progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: C14, C8, G03a, C13, C6b, C3 and Year 11: Ksp expressions, molar solubility and each ion as its count times s (C14); Q compared with K and the log number line (C8, G03a); solubility rules, spectators and net ionic equations (C13); dropping a tiny s with a 5 per cent check (C6b); Le Chatelier's principle (C3, C4); n = cV and mL to L (Year 11). Not assumed: Qsp, dilution on mixing, the common ion effect, Module 6 acid-base ideas.
progression.startsWith: A kidney stone made mainly of calcium oxalate, which the solubility rules call insoluble, and the question of how many ions are enough for a solid to form.
progression.stopsAfter: Finding each ion concentration after mixing from moles over the total volume; writing Qsp with the Ksp powers; comparing Qsp with a referenced Ksp to predict and justify a precipitate or none; explaining the common ion effect as Qsp exceeding Ksp with Ksp unchanged; calculating the solubility of a 1 : 1 salt in a common ion solution with the approximation checked. No titration methods, no selective precipitation, no temperature calculations, no Ksp from mixing data with the precipitate subtracted.
progression.nextLesson: Module 6, acids and bases (route chem-m6-acid-base-route), where K returns as Ka.

teaching.task: Predict whether a precipitate forms when two solutions are mixed, and say what a common ion does to solubility.
teaching.causalExplanation: A solid needs enough ions, so insoluble ions can coexist without one. Qsp is the Ksp expression with the concentrations right now, with the same powers. When Qsp is bigger than Ksp there are more ions than a saturated solution can hold, so they lock together until Qsp falls to Ksp, when it is just saturated, and when Qsp is smaller nothing precipitates. Mixing spreads each ion through the combined volume, so concentrations fall before Qsp is calculated, which is why moles are found first and divided by the total volume. A common ion raises Qsp above Ksp, so solid forms and less stays dissolved, while Ksp itself is unchanged because only temperature changes it. With a common ion present the initial row is not zero, and the tiny s is dropped next to it and checked.
teaching.conversationalApproach: Opens on a kidney stone and the question of how many ions are enough, defines Qsp and the three outcomes on a log number line, shows mixing spreading the ions, works a no-precipitate example with the undiluted trap and an unequal-volume example through moles, gives the memory aid, explains the common ion effect and calculates it with a non-zero initial row, then asks two unseen items with a short pause and brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: Most kidney stones are calcium oxalate, which the rules call insoluble, and urine always contains calcium and oxalate ions. Yet usually no stone forms. How many ions is enough?
teaching.understandingCheck: 20.0 mL of 1.0 x 10^-3 mol/L lead nitrate is mixed with 30.0 mL of 2.0 x 10^-3 mol/L potassium iodide, with Ksp 9.8 x 10^-9: will a precipitate form? Then solid sodium sulfate dissolves in a saturated calcium sulfate solution at the same temperature: what happens to the amount of calcium sulfate dissolved and to Ksp?
teaching.curriculumScope: Predict the formation of a precipitate given the standard reference values for Ksp (Module 5, 2017 syllabus p51). The common ion effect is taught as a Qsp consequence for one 1 : 1 salt. Titration methods, selective precipitation, temperature calculations and Ksp from mixing data with the precipitate subtracted are deferred.

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer, the painted kidney stone, saturated and unsaturated beakers, the painted pipette and clear no-precipitate tube, the C8 log number line with a fixed teal Ksp marker and a coral Qsp marker, the C14 ICE table, the C6b check ruler, the C13 swap-cross thumbnail, a coded mixing card and the countdown ring. Colour key: positive ions amber, negative ions violet, water shells pale blue, spectators grey, Ksp teal, Qsp coral.
design.transitionPlan: The kidney stone opens the lesson and returns small at the end; the two cards give way to the log number line, which carries the decision and every comparison; the beakers tip together for the mixing scene; each worked example clears to the same three-zone board; the saturated beaker carries the common ion scenes into the ICE table; each attempt clears the board and its feedback rebuilds the mixing card or the lens; the next chip slides in; scene crossfade with settle.
